tech-ai.title: AI on the Ballot
tech-ai.content:
AI on the Ballot 

 Wednesday, November 4, 2026 

 Listen to Podcast 

 Watch on YouTube 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 Listen to this post : 

 
 

 
 
 
 Log in to listen 

 From Bloomberg this morning at 2 a.m. Central:

 
 Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in a midterm election landslide that amounted to a rejection of President Donald Trump following widespread voter discontent with the economy and the war in Iran. Across the country, Democrats scored victories in GOP strongholds, flipping at least seven Senate seats and winning House races in districts Republicans easily carried in 2024. Several news organizations projected that Democrats would win the House, while Decision Desk HQ projected they took the Senate.

 

 I have no doubt that Iran and the economy played significant roles in this election; what stood out to me, however, was very much Stratechery fodder. Specifically, I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite.

 Meanwhile in Texas, from Yahoo Finance :

 
 A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state’s first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies. The state is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers…Hinojosa, Texas’ first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030.

 

 Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, I would note, already declared a moratorium on new data-center permits in September; that’s how much of a hot-button issue this is, including in the state that is the biggest opportunity and beneficiary of the data center buildout. So yeah, this is a Stratechery topic of concern.

 The Data Center Veto

 Earlier this year, while writing about data center opposition , I said:

 
 There really wasn’t widespread opposition to data centers when they were being built for the Internet generally; indeed, local governments would compete for them, eager for the economic benefits that came during their construction and the long-term tax benefits once they were operational. In other words, it seems pretty clear that the current wave of opposition can’t be divorced from AI — you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race.

 I do not, I don’t think, need to explain to you why this is not a very compelling message, and, in the very long run, I do think that humans will have economic value . At the same time, it’s hard to explain the huge amount of investment that is going into AI, not just at the model level but also in terms of data centers, without admitting that a big part of the thesis is that AI can not just increase the top line for companies, but also increase the bottom line — i.e. replace the jobs of some number of humans. Again, I’m generally an optimist here, but this already happened with the first wave of IT .

 That leads to an interesting contrast to globalization: when companies were closing down American factories and laying off workers and moving operations to China, none of the affected towns or workers had a say. They just suddenly no longer had a job, and a huge number of cities across the Rust Belt no longer had a reason to exist. People simply had to move, or worse, retreat to things like alcohol or drugs. AI, however, is the opposite: building data centers requires permission, which is to say that people actually have a say. Again, I am not at all saying that these people are well informed about data centers, or about the economic impact on their communities, much less the economic impact of AI generally; what I am noting is that people who didn’t have a say in globalization are suddenly finding they do have a say about AI, and it’s not a surprise they are expressing their disapproval by blocking data centers.

 

 That message was loud and clear last spring; now it is deafening, and it’s tempting to say that tech, particularly the frontier labs, have no one to blame but themselves. In fact, however, some of the biggest culprits may, in the long run, be some of the biggest beneficiaries of the anti-data center wave.

 My thesis — driven not just by national results and the Texas governorship, but also the fact that, as this thread documents , nearly every relevant local ballot measure opposing data centers won or is winning ( the only exception so far was in North Dakota ) — is that the constraint on AI dispersion has shifted once again. First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified. The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all. Not only is it harder to solve, but it actually interferes with solving the other constraints. Many of the theories about AI assume that it becomes a commodity; I think it’s just as likely we are looking at scarcity for much longer than we expected, which will have ripple effects on everything.

 Ten Takes

 To that end, here — with the caveat that nothing leads to hot takes you regret like an election — are ten perspectives on what a permanently impaired ability to build might mean. To be clear, I’m not declaring permanency — look at how our elections swing back and forth — but it’s worth considering what the implications might be if Americans don’t change their minds about data centers.

 1. The AI Trade Got It Right

 The most obvious reason why the stock market has been rocky over the last few weeks is the tightening of credit markets, which I wrote about this summer . We are, needless to say, full on into the equity funding era (and while I’m here, I haven’t written about Anthropic’s updated S-1 , but it strongly affirms my initial analysis ). At the same time, it seems clear that this outcome is very bad for the AI trade in the short term, but much of the pain may have already been endured.

 2. Neoclouds on the Edge

 The Neoclouds have been at the forefront of credit concerns, and from a certain perspective, being unable to build data centers has a silver lining in that they couldn’t get the money to pay for them anyways. Moreover, Neoclouds with facilities that are already permitted now have an asset that is going to be scarcer than expected. At the same time, it’s Neoclouds that need new sites and new permits, even as they are likely to have much less political sway than the hyperscalers — who already have more sites they can repurpose or rebuild. It was already getting harder to get capital, relative to the hyperscalers; now you have to layer on that it’s going to be harder to get permission, too.

 3. Hyperscalers Are Winners

 The downside for the neoclouds is upside for the hyperscalers, who are more likely to grow their share of AI compute than they were before. Moreover, investors may be pleased if the hyperscalers’ ambitions are somewhat curtailed; political opposition is an excuse to moderate spending, knowing that everyone else is in the same boat.

 4. Nvidia’s Mixed Bag

 Nvidia will almost certainly be a short-term loser. Fewer data centers mean fewer Nvidia chips generally, and a weakened Neocloud set is particularly harmful not only because Neoclouds almost exclusively use Nvidia full-rack systems, but also because Nvidia is back-stopping a huge number of them. It’s the hyperscalers, meanwhile, who are Nvidia’s biggest long-term threat, given their scale and ability to invest in their own chips.

 At the same time, a constrained world makes Nvidia’s offerings more compelling. CEO Jensen Huang actually spent an entire keynote making this point back in 2025; I wrote in an Update :

 
 When Huang says “iso power” he means that power is the constraint; the question is how many tokens can you generate given a fixed power envelope, and Blackwell can generate a lot more. These were the numbers Huang gave for a 100 MW data center:

 

 What this means is that the first order of business for an ASIC maker is to match that level of efficiency. That, though, means keeping up with Nvidia’s product development cadence; The Information has a post about Amazon offering instances using its latest Trainium ASIC at a significant discount to the H100. Huang, though, spent this keynote insulting the H100! You can almost hear him speaking to Amazon directly: you spent all this money, and are offering these huge discounts, just to entice developers to lock themselves into an inferior chip, even as reasoning models are going to swamp your available power generation…

 Huang is issuing a challenge to every cloud provider tempted to make an ASIC: do you really think that you can keep up with this, and risk running out of power capacity because your chips aren’t efficient enough? Don’t even try.

 

 A world without power or data center constraints is one where it is, in the very long run, very difficult to maintain Nvidia’s margins; once those constraints start to bite, however, an advantage in tokens/megawatt is worth a lot of money. Go back to my point about the hyperscalers: one way to generate more tokens is to build a new data center; another way is to rebuild a data center with new Nvidia chips.

 5. Advantage China

 China is the inverse of the scenario that Huang laid out: the country has plenty of power and the ability to build a lot more, but they don’t have leading-edge chips. Some of the advantages of leading-edge chips, however, can be overcome by simply throwing tons of electricity at the problem. From a 2025 Update about the Huawei CloudMatrix 384 supercomputer:

 
 The CloudMatrix 384, which is a supercomputer consisting of 384 chips, takes up dramatically more space, uses dramatically more power, is almost certainly dramatically more expensive to make, and is dramatically more brittle than Nvidia’s NVL72; there is no one in the world who would choose the CloudMatrix 384 over the NVL72 if they had the choice.

 That’s the thing, though: China doesn’t have the choice, because of U.S. export controls. The country’s saving grace is that they are operating on different constraints than the U.S.…China — which actually builds power generation — is not iso power; they are iso compute: Huawei’s goal with the CloudMatrix 384 is to get as much compute as possible, power efficiency be damned.

 

 In the fullness of time — i.e. as China figures out leading-edge chips — this may be an insurmountable advantage.

 6. Data Centers in Space

 When SpaceX released their S-1, I explicitly pointed to political opposition to data centers as one of the company’s most significant upside scenarios:

 
 The third question about data centers in space is if there is a stick. Specifically, while I think that racks-in-space are both a lot more viable than people think, and a lot more relevant to agentic inference than current modes of compute, it is at the end of the day cheaper and easier to build on earth, all things being equal.

 All things are not equal, however: right now we are at the very beginning of the AI buildout and already one of the biggest constraints is not just power (expected), but zoning (unexpected). I wrote in an Update last week:

 

 I already posted the relevant excerpt above. Continuing:

 
 In that Update I made the case that data center builders — and by extension the companies that use them — should straight up pay people for permission to build data centers in their communities. At a minimum, however, that increases the costs of terrestrial data centers. What seems very plausible in the long run is that the demand for compute ends up being so large that there eventually is nowhere left to build, making the vast expanses of space not just an alternative but in fact the only choice.

 

 This is where I come back to my experience watching these campaign ads: this isn’t a partisan issue, where the pendulum will swing back in two years. Both parties see opposition to data centers as a winning cause, and not just nationally: that thread has multiple examples of local officials straight up recalled for approving data centers in their localities. Space will be incredibly difficult, but difficulty is all relative! Moreover, to the extent opposition is permanent, the more this actually reduces the risk of data centers in space, because investors will have more confidence in there being enduring demand.

 7. The Frontier Labs Benefit

 If the hyperscalers had a red queen problem , the frontier labs have it even worse: the biggest revelation from Anthropic’s S-1 was that their inference margins were very high (good!), which meant that their massive compute costs were actually in R&D; this is bad because that R&D spend is governed by competition with the other frontier labs, and absent constraints, that spend looked set to surpass revenue sooner rather than later. Now, however, it is the public that is effectively demanding that the frontier be paced, which is great for the frontier labs’ financial outlook.

 The upside goes further than that: the point about efficiency being more important in a world of constraints doesn’t just matter for chips, but also for models. Devoting limited compute to inefficient and costlier-to-serve Chinese models is a poor trade if there isn’t enough compute. Moreover, open models may be at greater regulatory risk, as Democrats seem much more likely to pass laws that ultimately favor the frontier labs.

 There are some counter-arguments. First, if compute is constrained, and thus more expensive, then that will increase the drive to right-size models for jobs, which is a big argument in favor of open models; the fact that compute won’t be a commodity means that the frontier labs’ lower cost to serve will never come to bear on the low end of the market. And, it’s worth noting, it will be harder for the frontier labs to build their own compute, leaving them dependent on the hyperscalers; big tech wins again.

 8. Apple Gains

 The most obvious advantage for Apple is that in a world of constrained compute, inference on the edge will be that much more important. Another advantage is that any slowdown in the dispersion of AI is good for a company that dominated the previous paradigm .

 The biggest advantage of all, however, is that any slowdown in the AI buildout offers hope that the memory crunch will ease. This will take a while, to be sure, but no company would be a bigger beneficiary of the world running out of places to put AI chips than Apple.

 9. Startups Suffer

 AI has drawn a great many battle lines, not just in terms of data centers, but also within AI, and between AI and the rest of tech. Specifically, anything that strengthens the frontier labs is likely bad for the rest of the startup ecosystem. In a world with fewer data centers, startups will have less access to cheap compute, even as a slowdown in capabilities both means it takes longer to build compelling products and also gives the frontier labs time to actually build products that secure their ownership of the end user.

 10. The Human Factor

 One major fear that investors have had about the data center buildout is that there would be too much capacity, causing prices to plummet and investors and creditors to lose their shirts; that scenario, however, would be great for users, who would suddenly have access to incredibly cheap compute. Of course most users aren’t going to use AI directly; what they will miss out on is the equivalent of the Web 2.0 wave of free Internet services that were predicated on compute being free. Now there’s a good chance that AI is going to have meaningful marginal costs for a long time to come.

 At the same time, while I have been an optimist about humans in an AI future , there is no question that we were and are facing a wrenching change as intelligence becomes a commodity. It follows, however, that if it doesn’t become a commodity — or if that change takes longer than expected — that humanity will have more time to adapt. Maybe this is a break we needed; what is increasingly clear is it’s the break Americans wanted.

 That noted, there is a long history of citizens demanding the ends and opposing the means, and it’s the demand that wins in the end. The big difference today is that, unlike the first few waves of tech, the industry is going to need to do some convincing, and break the habit of assuming everything it does will get the benefit of the doubt. AI wasn’t technically on the ballot, but it was implicitly, and will be forevermore.

 
 

 Presented by

 

 I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy.

 Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating.

 

 Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them.

So the problem with something like the Mag Seven is there'll always be another company that soars that you wanna add on and say, "Look how well this company…" There's a selection bias here, and that's why when we started this and we said the Mag Seven are taking a big chunk of-- there's almost a selection bias that's gonna make that true. The Mag Seven might have a different acronym and a different-- maybe it'll be the Mag 10, it'll have a different front name. But almost by definition, because we're adding the most successful companies in the market to that space, if you did the backward test, it's gonna look like these 10 companies accounted for a big chunk in value. So be careful about modifications, because when that modification is made, it'll make it se-self-fulfilling in terms of, hey, these companies have carried the market. So the notion that the Mag Seven has carried the markets is often based on data, and the data seems to back it up, but I'm not sure that data can lead to us saying, "Okay, all I have to do then is buy these companies and I'm gonna be okay as an investor." That's the worst conclusion you can come to because it's an entirely backward-looking definition of success. This kind of goes into your story expertise more than your mathematical financial analyst expertise, but what is your take on what do you think slows AI first? Do you think it's gonna be regulation, or do I dare say some form of a disaster that's gonna slow us down? I hope it's regulation because, I mean, it could, could be a disaster. I don't think AI is embedded enough in companies for it to be a corporate disaster yet, but it could be a government disaster to the extent that AI is in governments, it's in intelligence agencies, it's in the, it's in the military. There's in-- The, the disaster then will be that AI will ask you to bomb a building that it tells you is full of munitions, and it turns out to be a building full of children, right? So it's, there-- I, I would rather that it be regulation because that disaster is gonna come at human cost that I think it's, uh, they're gonna be pretty catastrophic for us to pay attention in a world where, you know, things have become so easy to ignore and move on from. what are you watching, I'll call it a signal that other financial analysts or just the general population is completely ignoring? What do you think you might be seeing or looking at that, that I'm not thinking about or other, other financial analysts I'll make a confession. I don't follow markets closely. I don't watch CNBC. I don't read what analysts say. I live in San Diego. You know, right after this, I'm gonna go look after my granddaughter. I'm gonna pick her up from daycare, take her to the zoo for a couple of hours. I mean, I, I have this lu- I have the luxury of basically being disconnected from markets, and that to me is an advantage because when you're in New York and you follow markets constantly and you watch CNBC, it's very difficult to have perspective. So when that correction comes, as we, as we've agreed, there will be a correction, stay away from media, stay away from the expert advice because all you're gonna get is chaos in the moment, advice that's gonna be very short-term and often bad advice. So one advi- one piece of advice I'd give for everybody is have a plan for when the correction comes that's in place, preferably automated, which is put limit sells on things. If this happens and this happens, I'm gonna limit sell and convert to cash. Take it out of your hands because if you keep that decision in your hands and the crisis happens, you will find yourself paralyzed. Why? Because in the face of maximum uncertainty, human beings stop acting, and we all have to be aware of that. It's, it's part of-- it's built into our genes to panic because everybody else is panicking, and you want to try to kind of create processes that'll act for you when you're unable to act Well, and there my last question for you, and you touched on this a little bit. It's kind of what keeps you up at night kind of question. Um, I'll ask it a little bit differently. What do you worry about right now that you hope you're, you hope you're wrong about? That my grandchildren will l- be-- will live in a world where they will not be reasoning because you can look up the answer in ch- on ChatGPT, where every moment of every day is filled with stuff that they're told is s- important stuff, and they don't get a chance to let their minds wander. The things that make us human are the things that have allowed humanity to find ways to advance, and I have a feeling that we're disarming ahead of the threat by essentially not doing the things that allowed us to make those great discoveries in the first place. I'm less concerned for myself. Uh, my days are, you know, on the, uh, uh… I've done the bulk of my living. But I worry, as I said, for my grandchildren because they're going to be growing up in that world, and I wonder how it's going to shape. So if I lie awake at night, it's never, uh, li- it's never worrying about markets. It's either worrying about the Yankees winning their knockout game or worrying about my gra-grandchildren living in a world that's dystopian in terms of what they're asked to do. I appreciate that very much so. Um, where should people find you? I, I know mu- I mentioned Musings on Markets. Where do, where do you suggest people go to find you? Luckily, I have an unusual name. So if you type in my name into Google, you'll see my webpage, you'll see my blog, you'll see my YouTube channel. So everything is findable and, uh, you know, so I should be easy to find Fantastic. We'll be sure to link it as well. Aswath thank you so much. O- once again, just fantastic, um, just being able to make some sense of it for the, for the rest of us, as we like to say, and, and taking the complexity into more storytelling. So thank you for that Thank you Listen, if you enjoyed this conversation, it made you think, please subscribe, follow, join us on Substack. Um, and please, as we always like to say, until next time, uh, stay curious. Thanks again, Aswath.

business.title: If UPI Is Free, Who Pays for It? | PhonePe, Razorpay & NPCI | WTF is Payments?
business.content: [Nikhil] The entire history of money has been one move, repeating. Money keeps getting lighter. It started as grain and cattle, something you grew or herded, or could physically run out of. Then, it became gold coins stamped by kings, so heavy with meaning that entire empires ran on the weight of it. Gold became paper, a promise, instead of the metal itself. Paper became plastic. And, in India, money became a sound. The next move for money might be the strangest one yet. Something I've asked so many people, but nobody knows clearly. If you were to ask an AI data centre person, he would probably say money is moving to energy. I don't know which way this will play out. Maybe there is a business to be built around betting what that change might be. Grain, gold, paper, plastic, stablecoin, things on the blockchain, and I'm sure it'll change tomorrow as well. Today, I'm talking to people who built the last version of this story, the people who turned money into a sound. Sohini is the ED of growth at NPCI, the organisation behind UPI. Harshil Mathur is the co-founder of Razorpay. Sameer Nigam is the CEO and co-founder of PhonePe. We'll get into their journeys, the wins, the losses, the years nobody was watching, and where the next move in this history gets made. Because if you want to understand how India spends, or how to build the next big thing in this country, there's no one better place to teach you than the three people who will be sitting across from me today. Should we start by drawing a diagram of the different kind of payments and map out how it began? Okay, thank you guys for coming and doing this. So, let's begin with introductions, and who would like to go first? Okay, I can go first. We'll start from the very beginning. So, I was born in Rajasthan, went to this lovely school in Jaipur, school and college both, actually, initially, in Jaipur, and then went, did my MBA at this exclusive college for defence personnel and their dependents only, Symbiosis in Pune. Joined a bank, Axis Bank, spent... spent about 18 years doing lots of interesting non-core bank kind of things. So, all of payments, all of digital, all new initiatives. So, you know, I think that was kind of the grounding. Then went and-- Oh, before that, actually, in college, met my boyfriend and then now husband, my husband for more than 25 years now. -Then went to-- -What's his name? Siddesh. Yeah. Is he a regulator? -[Sohini] No. -[laughter] More the moderator than the regulator, I think. But yeah, then I worked in Western Union, the money transfer company that took me across the shores, spent some time learning about a lot of different countries and the way businesses are run there. And almost like, full circle, came back last year... to come and lead growth for NPCI, which actually can be a little interesting because... How do you grow a company which is already doing, like, roughly a billion transactions a day? So, I'm still figuring that one out. Is it a government posting or is it like private sector? You know, that's a very interesting question. Almost everybody asked me that question when I was joining as well to say, "So, are you going to be working for the government?" My father wanted to know if I'll get a white Ambassador with the Ashoka Stambh on it or not. Unfortunately, no. So, this was formed by RBI and IBA. So, it's set up as a not-for-profit. And yes, there is an element of us working-- Because it's a digital public infrastructure, so we work closely with the government and the regulator. It's a Section 8 company, right? -Yes, it's set up as a not-for-profit. -Who funds it? So it was set up with an initial funding of 100 crores. -By? -By ten banks. And now, actually, after that, it has generated enough surplus because it's not profit and it's not returned back to the shareholders, but all of the growth and the investments and the tech and the infrastructure and everything has been kind of self-funded. -Do Section 8 companies have shareholders? -Yes. And who are your shareholders? -Banks, fintechs, yes. -[Nikhil] You are? So, initially, we had to invite people to be our shareholders. Why? Because, initially, when it was just an idea, and it was just like-- It started with saying the ATM transactions, like the NFS, which was the National Financial Switch, which was set up to say that is some part which will be done by this company. -So, it's a long journey, where-- -But, as a shareholder, does Sameer make money on NPCI shares if you do well? So, because we don't return any money back to shareholders in the form of dividend, the surplus just goes into, like, the corpus for investments. -Right. -So, but at this point of time, -we are not set up like that. -Can you change like that? Can you change from Section 8? -I know OpenAI did something like this. -Yeah, yeah. So, technically, can you and "can you" can you are different questions, Nikhil. -So, technically, maybe yes. -Would you like to, if you had to choose? I think it's a "point in time" question. -At what point in time? -Now? Now, maybe not, because now I think there is still a lot that needs to be done. And to take the... to take the focus away on saying, "Hey, your main aim is to return value back to the shareholders," will take it away from the purpose. What if it becomes half the aim? -What if it becomes? -Half the aim. Like, a part of the money is returned back to shareholders. I don't think there are any half measures there, Nikhil. Like, the mandate that we have at this point of time, I think it's important that we continue on that journey. I'm also asking you for myself, 'cause I'm in fintech. I'm thinking, "How much can I pull your leg? Will you rap me tomorrow if I say something?" -[laughter] -Are you the regulator? -The reason both of us are a little quiet. -Are you independent? -Yeah? -Come on, Harshil. No, but, you know, I have to answer this one because... We are not the regulator. You will get us in trouble by calling us the regulator. There's only one regulator, and that's the Reserve Bank of India. But you know, this happens in stock broking, where NSE is not a regulator, but they can act like a regulator. -Ah. -They have some power to be a regulator. They're almost like a private regulator. They're not Section 8. -They're very different from you. -[Sohini] Yeah. But you must have some power that the Razorpay and PhonePe guys do not have, right? Um... I want to look at their reactions first. No, but you know what? The way we operate-- -Okay... -[laughter] No, so the way we operate is through steering committees, like, you know, so every decision-- And it's very difficult because of the fact that now, at this stage, there are lots of differing... priorities, right, for the different constituents of even the steering committee. Initially, obviously, everybody was at the same size, same scale, same... Now, there are lots of pushes and pulls, but most of our decisions still get taken through a steering committee framework. If Harshil does something that really bothers you, like something bad, what can you do to him, either directly or, like, you know, through someone? -I'll give you an example. -Okay. If there is-- If, on a particular app, frauds increase, okay, because they haven't put in some controls, so, our way of penalising will be, you cannot onboard new customers anymore now, -till you go back and fix it. -That's a big penalty. No, but that's important because that, like-- Unless you go fix this, you cannot onboard new customers. It's not like, hey, penalty in the sense of, like, you know, financial penalty or anything. -This is a financial penalty only... -It is. ...if you can't onboard new guys. Yeah, but it's important that you go and fix what needs to be fixed. So it will have to be something of the order of your risk controls not being adequate. I think that's needed as a-- For security of the system. -'Cause finally-- -You will obviously have to say that. [laughter] If someone else is doing it, it'll affect me, I will also suffer. Right. But accountability, finally, is to the Indian public. It's the vulnerable who get defrauded. So we have to-- -we have to take care of that. -Okay. But you have done a lot across the spectrum of payments, in a way. What did the Axis Bank experience teach you? A lot of things, actually. Are banks becoming irrelevant? I've thought about this. To a certain extent, regulation is harder for them... to compete on a fair queue. Like, if I'm trying to borrow money on the back of, say, private equity, a bank is not allowed to lend. I have to go to an NBFC. Like that, in many departments, banks are over-regulated or regulated so much more than a fintech player that that less regulation itself becomes a moat for fintech players. There are many ways to look at that, Nikhil, because, see, why are-- See, this is-- You're taking one part of it in isolation, because if you look at it, banks have to be regulated because the NBFC is not... taking deposits from the customers. The fact that you're taking the public money and then you're doing XYZ with it, you have to be regulated. So, you know, yes, this you can say that's the moat for the fintechs, but then there are other moats for the banks, and banks have got to leverage and work on their moats to be able to do that. Just cost of capital, no? Do they have any other moat? No, there's cost of capital, there's also-- And even in that, like, what, 2%-3% lower? It's not just about 2%-3% lower. The fact that they have that access which others do not have, like why did payment banks fail? -Again, regulation, I think. -No. Payment banks failed because you couldn't take... -Above one lakh, right? -You couldn't lend, you couldn't, yeah, your deposit taking capacity-- But there was regulation, no? -You can't take money above 1,00,000? -Exactly. -So, that model failed. -No, that's retail. You can take corporate deposits, those are larger, but you can't lend, or you can't... I think it's the same balancing act. If you can't take public money, you can't do this, then you are less regulated as well. If you take public money, you're also more regulated, so it's a-- Are payments banks dead? Like, I know Airtel is still running it. -Airtel is the one doing decent. -Airtel is the one, India Post is the one that is-- India Post wanted to exit or something like that was going on. Yeah, I think India Post because, again, of the structural-- That's the only one that is alive now, and there's Airtel. -Airtel is doing well. -And Jio Payments Bank which, again, I'm not sure whether they're not-- Even the SFB licencing didn't work out, right, small finance bank? Actually, that's worked out better. That's worked out better. -Why is that? -[Harshil] They can lend. Because they started with lending. They could lend. But they have some rule that you have to allocate... -Priority sector, yeah. -...30-40%. Banks also have priority sector rules, they have just higher priority sector rules. If you take a Slice today, that's an SMB. If you take a Shivalik, that's an SMB. So, priority sector is, I think-- Especially in the digital age, getting access to tier-2 and beyond customers is not hard. Is there a carrot at the end of that road that SFB will become universal? You can apply and convert. [overlapping conversations] -Is that what incentivises SFBs the most? -Yeah, yeah. I think that should be the-- Again, this is-- Especially the easier part in becoming a universal bank. Regulation also follows. You know, for a while we were trying to get a banking licence and when I spoke to the regulator, they showed me that Niti Aayog had made a white paper asking for a digital-only banking licence. [Sohini] Okay. It was a recommendation to the government that it should happen, but the people in the government then pointed to payments bank and said, "This is meant to be that, but this is not that." Yeah, this is not that. This is not that. See... Payment or digital only banks, so, this, you have to look at global examples. Many of the countries have done it and failed, like, even Southeast Asia, they tried to create this Grab Bank, GXS, etcetera. If you look at Revolut, which is like a... -roaring success, killing it, right? -Killing it! -[Harshil] Nubank. -Nubank, they got it right, but lots of other countries tried to go this route only, "We will give out licences." All of Southeast Asia, actually, "We will give out licences." And then they have all these conditions, then they make it a process, then there are three or four conglomerates which will come together. That never works out, no, so... But isn't there a case to be made to have digital only bank in India? There should be, there should be, yeah. -[Sameer] Lots. -That one, I think-- -You are kind of the regulator. -[laughter] You should tell, people will listen to you. Yeah. Right now, we find it difficult to make Harshil and Sameer listen to us. Just saying. [Sameer] Retail banking, we all know. So, he is admitting that, selectively, he'll listen to us... Okay. Harshil, would you like to go next? Sure, sure, and by the way, I didn't know you're from Jaipur. -I'm from Jaipur as well. -Wow, where? I grew up in Malviya Nagar, schooling from Seedling. -Okay, so I went to MGD. -Oh, nice. I mean, we spoke so many times, we didn't know we are both from Jaipur. I was born in Jaipur, grew up in an average middle class family in Jaipur. Dad worked in a bank. -Manager? -Banker. He was a clerk, actually. He became a manager by the time he retired. In SBI. And then, so, went to college in IIT Roorkee, was always-- Same, my dad. Became a manager around when he retired. Canara Bank. Yeah, close to two years before he retired. -Yeah, Canara Bank. -Yeah. Because you typically get posted out of the city -when you become a manager, so you-- -You get transferred every three, four years, right? Yeah, so that's why he avoided till retirement, till my schooling was done and all of that. So, yeah, went to IIT Roorkee, was always very deeply interested in computers from, like, school days, used to code stuff on the side. But unfortunately, I didn't make the rank in IIT, so I got into mechanical. Didn't know what to do with mechanical, had zero interest in it. You must have got like 99.2% instead of five, right? Yeah, I mean rank, rank. So I got a 1800 rank. You need to get under 1000 to get computer science. [Nikhil] Right. So, took mechanical, had zero interest in it. So, started forming this group of people who were interested in coding but couldn't do coding in their school time. And so we created a software group called Software Development Section. The group survives even today. So that's... So that was a college group where people would basically spend their time coding and building stuff. That was my first idea of building a startup of sort because I had to raise funding for it. And I can tell you, like, raising money from a government institution was harder than-- much harder than raising money from VCs. Because even if you do raise money, spending it is very hard. -You have to do tenders and all that. -So it is fairly painful. But that was my first experience of raising money. Now it's become hard to raise money from VC? I mean, raising money from VC is-- I'm saying it's much easier compared to raising from government institutions. Like, it is extremely hard. Every single rupee is audited, every single rupee is controlled. So it takes a lot of effort. You know one thing I didn't know about you? Black belt in karate. -[laughter] -Doesn't look like it. If I was in a fight, I wouldn't think, "Call Harshil." I don't know if it is a good thing or a bad thing. -No? -It sounds like a bad thing. -Would you have guessed? -I'm not messing with him. [laughter] I was a black belt. I actually got a silver in nationals. -[Sohini] Really? -What are you saying? Yeah. So, yeah, so then... So, at that point, I did learn how to, like, build stuff and things together. Met Shashank, my co-founder. So, graduated from college, again, because of mechanical got placed in Schlumberger, which is an oil company. Shashank was in Microsoft. And both of us talked that, "Man, I don't have any interest in this job. Let's try to build something of our own." So, while we were in our respective jobs, we used to keep building stuff on the side, side projects, like, doing something or the other for fun, like college. And for one of those things, we wanted to accept payments on that. So, we were building a social crowdfunding platform. Like, Facebook was very popular. So, we wanted a way for people to raise money for causes. More a side project, not a-- I would not say it was a startup. And for that, like, building the product was easy. The hardest problem was accepting payments. So we tried all the banks and the large payment players and all that and found it is extremely-- almost impossible to get through. It took us a couple of months. Even after we got an approval, the tech interface was extremely poor. Like, it was built for, I don't know, I'll say old school '90s world. And it felt like maybe we had a bad experience. So I started going to these-- Facebook was the most popular social media, so I would go to Bangalore startups, Pune startups, these Facebook groups, say, like, "How do you accept payments?" And everyone said, "Yeah, it's easier to accept cash, so just start accepting cash." I mean, Flipkart was, of course, the largest payment-- like, largest e-commerce company. COD was extremely popular. So, these are the five ways you can accept cash. Just go and accept in cash. That hit my techie brain hard. Like, the point of most tech is democratisation, right? So, like, Internet gives everyone access to information, social media gives everyone a voice. So, it didn't make sense to me that something digital is harder to do than something physical. So, it should be increasing access. So I started searching, researching online, "Why is that complicated? Why is it so painful?" And honestly, I couldn't find any real reasons for it. So, me and Shashank started speaking, "Should we try something in this?" And we had no idea of finance. My only exposure to finance was my dad used to work in a bank. -But beyond that, nothing else. -Which is no exposure. Which is no exposure. So, I remember I just walked into a bank branch next to my home on one of my off days, next to my home in Jaipur, and said, "I want to build." I learnt that payment gateway is a term used. So I said, like, "I want to build a payment gateway," and the guy said, "Do you want a payment gateway? I can give you one." "No, I said I want to build my payment gateway. How do I go about it?" And, of course, the guy had no idea. Nobody goes to a bank branch in Jaipur and says, "I want to start a payment gateway." So, connected me to somebody in Delhi. I spoke to that guy, explained what I want to do. He said, "No, you can't do it. Like, just get out of it." So, because, like, two 24 year, 25 year olds out of college, with no finance background, you don't just go and start a payment gateway. -Went to the next guy and so on. -Harshil is very proper, no? -Right? -Why proper? In the sense? Like, I have never seen you khul ke. -You know what I mean? -You have seen me khul ke, by the way. -When? -At your home. -Not fully khul ke, half khul ke. -Maybe you were also khul ke then. [laughter] -[Sohini] So you don't remember. -So you don't remember. -No, no, but I've not seen you like... -Unleash. Unleashed. Like, Sameer is always unleashed. -Yeah, that's true. -Yeah. -Okay. -Yeah. Why do you hold yourself back? I think it's a matter of company and time. Company, meaning, in front of me you tend to be like this? [stuttering] You have seen me. -[laughter] -There was a company then. Who was there? There were a lot of folks from Bangalore, the ecosystem and all that, so yeah, you have. There is an alter-ego. -There is a Fight Club moment. -Yeah. I feel the quietest ones are the craziest ones. [Sohini] Hmm. -[Nikhil] You know? -I kind of agree. -Yeah. -Right? [Nikhil] Yeah. Everybody has a mental picture going on now of Harshil doing crazy things. -I didn't agree because of me. -[Nikhil] I have one. -Now I have karate-crazy Harshil. -Karate. -Karate, pickleball and drinking. -I don't know what else will come out now. [laughter] -That's interesting, Harshil. -You tell me. What shall I say? I am-- Whatever you wish to say. I was born in Bombay into a naval family. My dad was in the Navy, small town guy from UP, went to IIT, naval architect. So, born here. I started my schooling in Germany. -Will you have some coffee? Black? -Absolutely. Yes, sir. -Coffee? Black? -Black is good. -Coffee, yeah. -Coffee is always welcome. Germany, yes. So that was interesting. I was, like, a four-year-old kid. I learnt German before I learnt English. -You still know it? -Very poorly. I understand more than I can speak. But the coolest part was, I think, at age 7, when they completed India's first submarine, we all got, families got invited. We sat in a submarine at age 7. I'll never forget that in my life. [Sohini] Wow. It's the only thing I remember, except German, besides German chocolates. Those are the two things I took away. Moved back to Delhi, spent about six years there. And then, at 13, I moved back as a teenager, moved back to Bombay. And it was the best damn place and time to move back. Early '90s was fun times in Bombay. We partied a lot. Met my co-founder now, Rahul, in undergrad. -Yeah, I think the best party. -There's no denial. So I was basically-- I was the serious one, Rahul was the party animal, if you've met him. No, I'm just kidding. He was through and through the brightest kid I knew in school. And I figured, "If I do something someday, I'll do it with this person." But dropped ship from there, went to the US. And, you know, at that time, I wanted a startup. I had no business skills and no background in my family, not even the banking part of it. Moved there, joined a startup after grad school in LA. The LA part was, I think, easy after Bombay. Partied hard, worked hard, worked in a startup, learnt the ropes, met my now wife there. When? What year? -We met on more than one road trip... -If you don't remember, it's okay. -...in 1999, 2000, 2001. -No worries. I'll make a reel about this and send it to your wife. No, no, there's many walks of shame there, don't worry. -They're captured in Polaroid. -Yeah? We partied out there, but virtually, yeah, it was really good fun. A company called ShopZilla, it was comparison shopping. I actually love just consumer Internet companies. This is the early days of the Internet. One of maybe first 10 clients that Google ever had, and Google broke after I had started working, and Yahoo and all these guys, so that entire hub, that was really good fun. Left in 2007, went to Wharton for a couple of years, started up my first venture. You can tell the Bombay and LA blood was there. So started a digital music company, went about aggregating music from all the Indian labels, and all the global labels, just basically, partying with all the studios. We never made any money. It had nothing to do with digital payments. They just never paid. [Sohini and Sameer chuckling] So, sales and collections are two different things. But we sold it to Flipkart in 2011. I moved to Bangalore, spent four amazing years there. -So, we saw their-- -Can I ask you a question? -Yeah. -In 2007-09, people went abroad, did MBA, a lot came back. Why are they not coming back now? I think, by '07... people, the first crop of people post-liberalisation who'd gone, had seen enough, and there was a view that India's digital moment will come. I think, right now, the macros are not in favour. I'm talking to a lot of young kids. My son's turning 18. They don't want to come back, no? I don't think that-- The middle-class aspirants don't want to be here. And I think it's sad. And, um, I mean, on a serious matter, I think it bothers me because I came back. I've had a great run, you've had a great run. But I think-- When you say macros are bad, what do you mean? I think there's a population of people that has grown up in the Insta world, in the YouTube world, that has seen what's possible out there. And they're seeing governments and markets opening up. And they're seeing... governments not sort of getting in the way of just unleashing animal instincts. And I think we are at an inflection point. We're at a weird inflection point. So, fine, PhonePe sent a message, "Nikhil, Canara Bank, Vrushank, HDFC Bank, rupees 100 transfer." That message went to the sponsor bank, PhonePe has touched no money. [Harshil] PhonePe doesn't touch money, anyway. The PSP or sponsor bank, Axis got it. They relayed that message to NPCI. -[Sohini] Yes. -Now what does NPCI do? So, NPCI now resolves because you sent-- today, you send money to people's phone numbers, right? Like, or to your contacts. So, NPCI resolves that number to say, "Hey, this now needs to go to HDFC Bank," and sends that information to HDFC Bank to confirm, "Yes, this is the right recipient," sends that message back to... PhonePe, back to, yeah, through Yes Bank. So PhonePe, in turn, is messaging HDFC Bank and saying, "Here is a credit entry of 100 rupees for Vrushank." -PhonePe is not. -[Harshil] PhonePe is not doing that. NPCI is calling HDFC Bank and saying that 100 rupees is transferred to Vrushank... -To Vrushank from Nikhil. -...from Nikhil. -But also, also... -So, it's mostly not just two things happening-- It's also checking with your bank account, -Canara Bank... -If the money is there. ...whether this money is there, because finally, money has to get debited from Canara to go here. How does this money actually move? Before the money... It's almost like, if you are using a Hotmail account and emailing somebody on a Gmail account. Right? That's money-- When you send money to a mobile number, that mobile number is linked to some app. -Right. -You're using PhonePe, but the other party could have last used a GPay or a Paytm or any other app. So, first is namespace resolution, which is what she was referring to. -Yeah, first NPCI... -Namespace. Yeah, which is your VPA... Virtual payment address. It's basically, I have a phone number, there's another-- Nikhil@okaxis, and I'm Sameer@ybl. Like a private number which other people can't see. So, first, those need to be translated -into bank... -[both] Bank account numbers. -...account numbers. -Who's doing that? That is where... starts with the PhonePe, goes to NPCI, bounces back with the resolution in place, -then we make a payment request... -[Sohini] Request and a response. ...which says, "On behalf of Nikhil, please move the money from Canara to HDFC. Here's his authentication detail." That's when the authentication happens. And NPCI is relevant because everybody from the sponsor bank to the authoriser bank to the receiver bank, everybody is sharing a API where you can talk to everybody. Otherwise, everyone will have to connect everyone individually. So, each transaction is roughly 10 API calls. And all of that is happening in, like... -less than... whatever. Milliseconds. -Milliseconds. Microseconds. Right. So, there is a cost here. You had asked the cost question. There is a cost for every entity, even your bank. -Canara Bank. -What is it? Is it like a data cost for your 10 API calls, which is the main cost? For PhonePe, GPay, Paytm, the apps, it's the cost of the banks. Because now, earlier, you were walking into a bank, withdrawing 5000 rupees, so that was one transaction. Now you're making 50 such transactions, so there's the core banking. For every transaction, the bank sends you a SMS. So, there's the bank, the PSPs, the apps, and if there is a merchant transaction which we haven't got into, the acquiring parties' costs, so that is the entire cost. Even before we go there, now my money has transferred from Nikhil to Vrushank, my Canara Bank to HDFC. How much has it costed? Everybody put together? Everybody put together, for the transaction? We had, I think there was some calculation that was done, -0.25%, roughly. -25 paisa? No, it's not 25 paise. I think if you netted out at an ecosystem level, it's about 25 bips. -Which is 25 paisa on 100 rupees. -On 100 rupees, yeah. Yeah, yeah, he said 100 rupees, so... P2P dynamics are different, retail dynamics are different, switching fees and all the other fees-- -Just let's stick to P2P for now. -Yeah. In this 25 bips cost, how much of the cost lies where? How much does NPCI spend on this? How much does PhonePe spend on this? How much do the sponsor and receiver banks spend? My gut says, and I could be wrong, the highest expense is borne between the... TPAP and the issuer, in this particular case. -The receiver has very little to do-- -What is TPAP? The third party app, PhonePe. PhonePe is the app and the issuer is Canara Bank, in your case. Because I think what's lost in this is, between the TPAP and the PSP, some are more tightly coupled, some are less tightly coupled. But we have to do the first factor authentication, your device fingerprint, right? -There's... -Which is what, one API call? No, that's on the edge, on the app. But then, we need to do a bucket load of fraud and risk checks in real time, -even before we go ahead to NPCI. -Like? Tons of things. For example, it's a very simple use case. Let's say you've done 100 transactions every month for the last three months. Suddenly, I find that... there's a transaction originating and it seems to be coming from you being in Raipur. -That's a flag. -Why? Because we need to verify. And again, you have to look at 20 other parameters in tandem. Now, do you look at this? It's on the edge. It's on the device. I don't think-- No, but do you look at only the client's data on PhonePe or do you get access to aggregate data of what I have done from Raipur -on PhonePe and GPay and 100 different-- -No. -So that, we do. -[Sameer] Networks have different rules on top. So we run a bunch of fraud and risk models which also are on top of all of this. So, you're the second level of check. Yeah, because we see and we run our FRM engines and our fraud models and all, because it's important to look at patterns across the ecosystem to see if there's very fast velocity of money moving from one hop to another, etcetera, so that's-- And these costs, and these costs change a lot in P2M world. [Sohini] Yeah, yeah. If you're sending or receiving money to the mobile number, the mobile number binding itself is important. The SIM binding is important. If I find that your device specs keep changing, that SIM seems to be travelling, we look at that. You introduce hurdles if you find different risk parameters going off the charts. So, there's a lot of that activity. There's just a lot of data to be captured and stored for verification, for chargebacks and other stuff as well. So you maintain a database somewhere. So, we have-- Actually, like, just at our scale, right? We have about 30,000 servers now. And it's the second largest data footprint in the country for CDP, -behind just Jio as a group. -[Nikhil] Right. That's how much data has to be retained also. And there's regulatory requirements, there's NPCI and market-- And when Nikhil is transferring money to Vrushank, is there a fee for the 100 rupee transfer? There is no fees to Nikhil. Nikhil's bank, Canara Bank, will pay our PSP bank somewhere between 15 and 50 paise, depending on the slab, because transfers go up to 1,00,000. Who pays that? The PSP. -The issuing bank pays the PSP bank. -Your bank, Canara Bank, in this case. Canara pays Yes Bank or Axis, whoever our partners for that transaction, -and we negotiate a share of that. -How much do they pay? It's a slab-based thing, and I think it caps at 50 paise? Where is that coming from? It's coming from Canara. It's coming from-- But why they paying it if they're not making anything? Because you have the convenience as their customer of doing easy digital transactions, which reduces their branch and ATM costs, or their NEFT costs, without them having done anything. Otherwise, they would have had -a cost of the transaction. -The cost of the ATM or something. So they're making money from the money lying idle in my account, -Yes. -The float income. -Which is, like, the bank-- -[overlapping conversation] It's a cost that they've saved, essentially. Like, if you had to give money to him, you would've technically gone to an ATM and withdrew cash. Actually, the reason I know it's 50 paise, It's their CASA Book in return for float? No, no, no, this is your customer servicing cost. Remember you used to into your net banking and do NEFT/RTGS? There, even though NEFT/RTGS are run by the regulator, as far as I know, they also charge the banks 50 paise on that transaction, so it's on par. In fact, your bank used to charge you five rupees for that 50 paise cost. Here, in fact, I think, yeah, NPCI's very benevolent, there's no markup. Okay, so the cost of this transaction is 25 bips. Outside of that, Canara Bank pays between 15 to 50 bips to the PSP, the person PhonePe is sending a message to, saying, "Do this transfer." -And this money is spent on? -This money is spent on tech. There's about 1,500-1,800 of employees... -[Harshil] Engineers. -...engineers, fraud models. We run, obviously, because of all of this money that is moving, we have to ensure that there is a settlement guarantee fund. So there is the entire treasury management of that, the money movement, all the other audits, regulatory functions. And because these transactions are instantaneous, there's no concept of float anywhere. Nobody gets to keep the money for a while before the receiver gets it. Yeah, no, this is unlike what you have in, say, China, etcetera, where the Alipay, WeChat, which are basically-- -They have a float part. -Those are wallet-based. This is a real-time instant payment system. So, money moves from-- The float is already either in your bank account or the other person's bank account. So, they are in any case meant to. Banks are meant to have the float. So, none of the other intermediaries. -The money doesn't stay. -See, earlier the bank who sent the money was making the float, now the bank who received is going to make the float. So, the float is made either way, but... the system is not taking the float. One of the coolest things about the NPCI architecture or UPI architecture is the real-time payment just basically-- is a accounting debit or credit that's happening, whereas they do the settlements out of bank. -Really? When does that happen? -Yeah. -After how much time? -That pool stays with UPI or with NPCI and then they settle, what, eight times a day now? -We settle ten times a day. -Ten times a day. So, it's a massive-- I would imagine a massive pool sitting there for the settlements. They're able to move that quickly because it's much more just about ledger management -than the money-- -When you say it sits at UPI, -it sits at NPCI? -NPCI. So, it's in the RTGS account in RBI. So you'd have to move it from bank A to bank B. You do that settlement, do that settlement file posting. You could have 100 million transactions in two hours in peak hour, but ultimately, the gross settlements would be like 800 settlements, 400 on either side at the end of the cycle. -You just do the net value. -[Sohini] Yeah. Brilliant architecture. That's a bit like how shares move in the US, right? The shares never get transferred, unlike India. Okay, so this is P2P. What was the other thing you guys were saying? P2M. -P2M. -That's a merchant transaction. -What changes? -[Sameer] The MDR comes in. Take an online merchant. [Sameer] A lot. -A lot changes. -[Nikhil] More complicated? -No, so, same actors. -[Sohini] More actors. But I'll tell you, I tried to research before this. There is no information about this anywhere. Like, there's so much, like, in pockets, but nobody even explains what is UPI, how does it work properly. Like, once we do this, we'll make an animation of every step of the way, who does what, how does it work, and then we'll put it out. -Yeah. -Interesting. But we were wondering if, if the aim is to see if some young people would be -starting-- -Starting, but, I don't know, we might end up scaring them that this is complicated. We are kind of not doing that job well, right? [Nikhil] In the end, we will. No, I am saying that for me as well, and when I got into payments, I was completely from unfamiliar-- So, slowly peeled it down, I realised that there is a lot of complexity in there. -From the outside, you don't see it. -[Nikhil] Yeah. You keep peeling the stack, you figure out that, "Oh, there is a lot more." And then you slowly start appreciating, "Okay, this is also needed." Because initially, I was like, "Why do I need this much? -It's a simple money flow." -But basics are not found anywhere. In the end, we'll go to it. We'll go to what Stripe is doing, what's happening with stablecoins. Is there opportunity in cross-border payment? Somewhere, somebody will build. I was interviewing this Coinbase founder, Brian Armstrong. He made a very strong case for stablecoins. In India, the dollar-based ones will not function, because... I don't think the government will allow it. But what about the use case for a stablecoin with something else backing it? Especially cross-border, I think there's a lot of problems to be solved. Yeah, see, nobody wants to hold rupee as paper because of how quickly it's depreciating. But if it could be based on a commodity that India holds, maybe there's an opportunity there. But we'll get into things-- Things like that people will want to build. But the one thing I realised with Brian is in that entire crypto world, the only thing that's left is Bitcoin and stablecoin. -Everything else is dead. -The value of the stablecoin will matter. Stablecoin takes away the speculation part. The problem with central banks across the world, is they're so in love with the concept of their CBDCs, which is a much more complex problem, I think, in ten years, you'll end up with peering of UPI with a lot of networks and Pix and all these other networks. Real-time networks peering will move much faster than CBDCs. -Because nobody will deliberately-- -It didn't work, no? Nobody's going to run on somebody else's CBDC. So we're still creating disjointed outcomes. Egos and prides come in, right? "My CBDC is bigger, their CBDC is bigger." Yes, yes, that, exactly. Disjointed. But what if government's CBDC comes out? That's what we're talking-- You're talking about for cross-border. I'm talking about internally for the country. Internally, UPI solves it. Why do you need it CBDC? -In India, we don't even need it. -UPI solves it. Solution waiting for a problem. Like, I can move and send money to you instantly, autonomously, smoothly, -in milliseconds, what do I-- -No, and by the way, I think-- See, if I think CBDC is a... is like a currency which is sitting on top of the rupee as the commodity underlying it, if I think the value of rupee is going down and if I can replace rupee with something else as a store of value, then something like CBDC could be interesting. No, but they never allow that. CBDC is one is to one with the rupee. Because then you are speculating. If it is speculative, then it's not a central bank backed. But what if I want to speculate? I want a gold-backed-- But like that we have Bitcoin. Then it becomes a Bitcoin itself. So, it is ultimately the central bank's promise that digital rupee has the same "I promise to pay the bearer" promise. The value of that cannot be mutated. But the value is mutated anyway. Anyways, it's moving up and down, right? The value of one rupee in a year will be something different. But you're comparing. Within the ecosystem, one rupee is one rupee. [Sameer] The underlying value of the rupee is fluctuating. -You're comparing it with the dollar. -It's being compared with the outside. -Internally, it runs within the system. -Internally, the rupee is the rupee. But see, if I take a CBDC today, one rupee, in one year, invariably, because of inflation and depreciation, the value of that asset class is lower. If I had a choice and I didn't want that one rupee for a year, I would pick a commodity to back that under versus... Then it's speculative. Then it's not a currency. -Then you can buy it for yourself. -[Sameer] That's the problem with crypto. That's why central banks hate crypto. And I think the reason that citizens don't like CBDCs, US is pretty much, Trump is banning it. Crypto is different because there's nothing backing it. No, even with the stablecoin, I'm saying that, ultimately, the reason the stablecoin solutions are working is that you know what it's spec to, you know underlying value. If you remove the value, then you're back to square one. A CBDC where the rupee-- If I have a five rupee CBDC in my hand and tomorrow I don't get back five rupees from the central bank in value, then it's not five rupees. But can I ask you this question? I know CBDC is backed to the dollar right now. No, that's a USDT. No, no, sorry, USDT, USDT, Stablecoins are backed to the dollar. CBDC is Central Bank Digital Currency. In India, it's rupee, in the US, it's dollar. [Sohini] Yeah. Now, I know for a fact that the Federal Reserve in the US is probably going to try and depreciate the value of the dollar -to reduce the debt. -Significantly. I mean they've announced it, they've said it once or twice, long term, it'll happen. I think even now it's happened versus other currencies, not versus the rupee maybe. So that is also volatility, right? If they are saying, on their own, that, "We'll depreciate the value of the dollar," and my USDT or whatever circle issues is backed to the dollar, it's volatile because the value of the dollar is going up and down. The way to manage that will be to park your money in an asset where you believe. But the currency cannot be the same thing. The currency needs my ability to send you money where you can trust the money that I am sending it to you. -If it's moving around, it becomes hard. -No, he's onto something. See, currency is a value of exchange. Yeah, the focus is exchange that I should be able to trust the money that I have sent, and it carries value. But I'm saying what you're saying-- what you're sending me as a dollar, the value of that exchange is changing for me. But you're making the use case specifically on cross-border, right? Like, if you are in the US and you have your 100 US dollars and you're not-- the value of that 100 US dollar within the US is the same, regardless of whether the US dollar is going to be-- Okay, just for this example, think I'm in India. And you're buying USDT. -So then, the use case is cross-border. -The origin of crypto was to-- Cross-border is a very different use case and there is a value. No, the origin of crypto was to get around central banks manipulating the value of the currency. Exactly that. The original spirit was very, very anarchic and awesome. That spirit broke because there was nothing underlying it. If the original set of cryptos was pegged, say, to gold, you went back to the bullion standard, then everyone's on the same currency. They weren't pegged. And central banks made damn sure across the world that they're right back to controlling the currency movement. Because if the central bank loses the ability, for example, to depreciate the dollar when they need to, or inflate the value when they need to, then the central bank loses all power. And the one thing I've learnt in life the very hard way is bankers never lose underlying intrinsic value, even if governments fail. They will never give up that power. And the same is true here as well. I mean, it's just-- anywhere you go, the promissory note is power. And if you can speculate against that, then they lose that power. In a way, that's happening in India even, as people are no longer parking money in banks and going directly into the stock market, for example. -Can I be provocative here? -Yeah. So, at heart, I like old school American capitalism, which is grounded in the concept that regardless of birth, enterprise in one lifetime, you can actually just become anybody you want to be. Yeah. I think capital markets are extremely distorted right now, globally, in that, money makes money way faster than labour makes money or enterprise makes money. And that's a global trend, which is why income disparities are out of whack. So, role of government, ironically, in the democracies is in need much more than ever. I feel that. -That said-- -But that is working in some places. In some places. There's something called the Gini coefficient, which measures income inequality. And in places like Australia, some Nordic countries, it is coming down. It's coming down by interventions around tax, largely. Some places have high property tax. Some people have some places have inheritance tax -that we should totally have. -Yeah. -I don't get-- -Progressive tax regime. If Sameer earns money in his lifetime, he should be allowed to do what he wants, but Sameer's son can pay 20% tax on what Sameer earned above a certain number before he inherits it. -Not just that-- -But those are the changes we can ask for, because those are pragmatic. I think capital gains, and the US will have to lead the-- I think they will end up leading the charge on this someday. Capital gains cannot be at a lower rate, just because it's private equity. The argument has always been private equity people will not invest in the market. Money will always get invested. Capital gains cannot be a fourth of income tax rates. But I think they're changing that. I'm saying if they lead, India will-- They're trying to put in a MAT which hits Cayman and Dubai and all these countries like a minimum alternative tax. If the US leads, India and others will look better. Today, we look regressive. -We look bad to the-- -We look regressive. Ours was zero earlier, it just happened. Amongst the global competition, the money will move out. You can't make it higher if the West and Singapore are lower, but if everyone gets there, everyone should agree... The only issue, so... NPCI-PhonePe, for example, right? I think, spiritually, very aligned on inclusion, for example. Where, I think, to his point, interference from a sourceless standpoint herd, let's take MDR six years ago. So, in 2018, we had brought this request to NPCI for what's called a P2PM. MCC code, a category code-- Every category has a code in payments. So, before the government announced zero MDR, PhonePe had almost 30 million QR codes in the market, but they were on the P2P rail. And the regulator finally agreed. They said, "Let India not charge the small kiranas." Up to a limit og one lakh rupees, there was... India is the only market, by the way, worldwide, which actually has a formal P2PM code. 0000. By the way, the people rejecting the most... I remember, in fact, Nithin being one of them and correctly so, saying, "Yaar, money moving into brokerage, you tax it when activity happens, you can't tax money transfer like that." There were brokerages, there were other transactions. -OMCs complained a lot. -Yeah. But there were exemptions that NPCI had introduced already. In fact, mutual fund transfers, IPO, they're all discounted. So, there are-- There is... So, you have to make those exemptions by use case pragmatically. See, I think... I think... it is a huge success now, right? Why are we shy about saying it? The data, the rate of growth of UPI transactions on the retail side, was higher, not lower. Bu rate of growth is a... Rate of growth is gonna keep coming down because the base is becoming bigger. But even if it was a segment, you could've applied it to, like, say P2P, they wanted to. You were not charging, but they were adding charges. They wanted to add rules... It would've made sense for specific sectors. Again, I'll give an example of online, right? Whenever MDR debit comes up, offline is talked about a lot. Online, very few people understand, because it's a very different ecosystem, runs differently. For an online merchant, the cost of cash is higher than the cost of a digital payment. So, there, why are you introducing... Because there is already incentive to move to digital. For
